pages.title: Basic Concepts
pages.content:
### Graph:
- Graphs are versatile data structures used to model relationships between entities. They consist of nodes (vertices) and edges. Graphs can be directed (edges have a specific direction) or undirected (edges have no direction). Graphs can also be weighted (edges have associated values) or unweighted.

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graphs-ds.jpg)
### Node (or Vertex):
- Nodes are used to depict individual entities or points in the context of the problem being modeled by the graph. Nodes can carry additional information, such as labels or attributes, depending on the application. In social networks, nodes might represent individuals, while in a road network, nodes might represent intersections.

![Node](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graphs-nodes.png)

### Edge:
- Edges represent relationships or connections between the entities represented by nodes. In an undirected graph, an edge is a two-way connection, whereas in a directed graph, edges have a specific direction from one node to another. Edges can also have weights, indicating the strength or cost of the connection. For example, in a transportation network, edges might represent roads, and the weight could represent the travel distance or time between two locations.

![edge](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/graph-edges.png)

pages.title: Graph Types - Undirected and Directed
pages.content:
#### Undirected Graph(or Bidirectional Graph):
- An undirected graph is a graph in which edges have no direction. The relationships between nodes are symmetric, meaning that if there is an edge connecting node A to node B, there is also an edge connecting node B to node A. 

Example: \
![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/undirected-graph-with-7-nodes-and-7-edges.png)
### Key Characteristics:

- **Symmetry:** Edges do not have a specific direction, indicating a mutual relationship between connected nodes.
- **Edge Uniqueness:** There is typically only one edge between any pair of nodes, regardless of the order in which the nodes are listed.
- **Example Scenario:**
Consider a social network where nodes represent individuals, and edges represent friendships. In an undirected graph, the friendship is mutual, and the graph captures the symmetric nature of friendships.

### Directed Graph (Digraph/Unidirectional Graph):
- A directed graph, or digraph, is a graph in which edges have a specific direction. Each edge points from one node to another, indicating a one-way relationship.

Example: \
![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/directed-graph-no-background.png)
#### Key Characteristics:

- **Directionality:** Edges have a clear direction, representing an ordered pair of nodes, where the edge starts from one node and points to another.
- **Asymmetry:** Unlike undirected graphs, directed graphs can have edges in only one direction between nodes or have edges in both directions.
- **Example Scenario:**
Consider a website where nodes represent web pages, and edges represent hyperlinks. In a directed graph, the hyperlinks direct traffic from one page to another, capturing the one-way flow of information on the internet.

pages.title: Connected, Disconnected and Weighted Graphs
pages.content:
### **Connected Graph:**

A connected graph is a graph in which there exists a path between every pair of nodes. In other words, every node is reachable from every other node by following the edges of the graph.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/connected-graph2.png)

**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Path Existence:** A path exists between any two nodes in the graph.
2. **Single Connected Component:** There is a single connected component, and no isolated nodes or subgraphs.

**Example Scenario:**
Imagine a transportation network where nodes represent cities, and edges represent roads. A connected graph ensures that there is a route between any two cities, facilitating seamless travel.

### **Disconnected Graph:**

A disconnected graph is a graph in which there are at least two nodes without a path connecting them. It consists of two or more connected components, each of which is a connected subgraph.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/disconnected-graph.png)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Isolated Nodes:** Nodes may exist without a path to reach other nodes in the graph.
2. **Multiple Connected Components:** The graph is comprised of two or more connected subgraphs.

**Example Scenario:**
Consider a social network where nodes represent individuals, and edges represent friendships. A disconnected graph may indicate the presence of isolated groups of friends with no connections between them.

### **Weighted Graph:**

A weighted graph is a graph in which each edge has an associated numerical value or weight. These weights can represent distances, costs, time, or any other relevant measure.

Example: 

![graph](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/weighted-graph.png)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Edge Weights:** Each edge is assigned a numerical value, indicating the significance or cost of the connection.
2. **Quantification of Relationships:** Weights provide a quantitative measure of the relationship between connected nodes.

**Example Scenario:**
In a communication network where nodes represent routers and edges represent communication links, a weighted graph can represent the latency or bandwidth associated with each link, allowing for optimization of data transfer.

callout.text: Use Connected, Disconnected and Weighted Graphs to build a precise mental model of Types of Graphs, then apply it in graph problems.

pages.title: Trees and Forests
pages.content:
In graph theory, trees and forests are specialized structures that arise from the arrangement of nodes and edges in a graph. Understanding these concepts is fundamental for modeling hierarchical relationships and detecting cycles within a graph.

### **Tree:**

A tree in graph theory is an undirected graph with the following properties:

1. **Connected:** All nodes are connected by edges, and there is a unique path between any pair of nodes.
2. **Acyclic:** There are no cycles or closed loops in the graph.

Example:

![tree](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/tree-data-structure.jpg)


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Root Node:** A designated node from which all other nodes are reachable. It has no incoming edges.
2. **Parent and Child Nodes:** Nodes in a tree are organized into parent-child relationships, forming a hierarchical structure.
3. **Leaves:** Nodes with no children in the tree are called leaves.

**Example Scenario:**
Consider a family tree, where each node represents an individual, and edges represent parent-child relationships. The resulting structure is a tree with a clear hierarchy and no cycles.

### **Forest:**

A forest is a collection of disjoint trees or, in other words, a graph without cycles. It can consist of one or more trees.

Example:

![forest](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/forest-tree-terminology.png) 


**Key Characteristics:**
1. **Disjoint Trees:** Trees in a forest do not share any common nodes or edges.
2. **Components:** Each tree in the forest is a connected component, and the entire forest may have multiple connected components.

**Example Scenario:**
In a computer network, nodes represent computers, and edges represent network connections. The absence of cycles ensures that there are no redundant or looping paths, creating a forest of disjoint trees.

pages.title: Graph Representations
pages.content:
Graphs, as fundamental structures in computer science and mathematics, can be represented in various ways to suit different applications. Three common representations are the Adjacency Matrix, Adjacency List, and Edge List. Let's explore each of these methods.

### **1. Adjacency Matrix:**

**Definition:** An adjacency matrix is a 2D array where the entry `matrix[i][j]` represents the presence or absence of an edge between nodes `i` and `j`.

**Explanation:**
- **Size:** The matrix is of size `N x N`, where `N` is the number of nodes in the graph.
- **Symmetry:** For an undirected graph, the matrix is symmetric since the relationship between nodes `i` and `j` is the same as between `j` and `i`.
- **Values:** If there is an edge between nodes `i` and `j`, `matrix[i][j]` (and `matrix[j][i]` in the case of an undirected graph) is set to 1; otherwise, it is 0.
  
**Example:**
Consider a graph with nodes A, B, and C. If there is an edge between A and B, `matrix[A][B]` and `matrix[B][A]` would be 1.

### **2. Adjacency List:**

**Definition:** An adjacency list is a collection of linked lists or arrays, where each node `i` has a list of its neighboring nodes.

**Explanation:**
- **Size:** The list contains `N` elements, one for each node in the graph.
- **Nodes and Neighbors:** Each element represents a node, and the associated list contains its neighboring nodes.
- **Flexibility:** Suitable for sparse graphs, as it doesn't require space for non-existent edges.

**Example:**
For the same graph, the adjacency list for node A might be [B, C] if there are edges connecting A to B and A to C.


### **Comparison:**

- **Adjacency Matrix vs. Adjacency List:**
  - Use an adjacency matrix for dense graphs with many edges.
  - Use an adjacency list for sparse graphs to save memory.

**Choosing the Right Representation:**
- **Adjacency Matrix:** Quick edge presence check, suitable for dense graphs.
- **Adjacency List:** Efficient for sparse graphs and efficient memory usage.

pages.title: Adjacency Matrix Definition
pages.content:
### Adjacency Matrix Definition

Common graph representations are adjacency matrices and adjacency lists. A matrix gives O(1) edge-existence checks but uses O(V²) space; adjacency lists use O(V+E) space and are usually preferable for sparse graphs.

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Graph Traversals.

pages.title: Graphs Traversal Algorithms
pages.content:
### **Graph Traversal Algorithms**

**1. Breadth-First Search (BFS):**

**Concept:**
Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that systematically explores a graph by visiting all the nodes at the current depth before moving on to nodes at the next depth.


**Applications:**
- Finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
- Detecting connected components in a graph.

**2. Depth-First Search (DFS):**

**Concept:**
Depth-First Search (DFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.

**Applications:**
- Topological sorting of directed acyclic graphs.
- Detecting cycles in a graph.

**Comparison:**

| `Criteria` | `Breadth-First Search (BFS)` | `Depth-First Search (DFS)` |
|----------|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Order**    | Level by level            | Depth by depth          |
| **Data Structure** | Queue               | Recursion or Stack      |
| **Path**     | Shortest path in an unweighted graph | Not necessarily the shortest path |
| **Memory**   | More memory intensive     | Less memory intensive   |



We'll learn more about each of these algorithms, in upcoming sections.

pages.title: Analysis of DFS
pages.content:
### **Time Complexity:**
- The time complexity of DFS is O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices (nodes) and E is the number of edges in the graph.
- Each vertex and edge is visited once in the worst-case scenario.

### **Space Complexity:**
- The space complexity of DFS is O(V) for the recursive implementation and O(V + E) for the iterative implementation using a stack.
- The space required is proportional to the maximum depth of the recursion stack or the maximum size of the stack.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use Analysis of DFS to build a precise mental model of Graph Traversals, then apply it in graph problems.

pages.title: Analysis of BFS
pages.content:
Each vertex takes $O(1)$ time to visit and to explore all $M$ edges we take $O(M)$ total time. \
So, the time complexity becomes $O(1 \cdot N + M)$, $O(N + M)$. \
Where $N$ is the number of vertices in the graph.

Since the queue size will be equal to the number of vertices at maximum, the space complexity is $O(N)$.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use Analysis of BFS to build a precise mental model of Graph Traversals, then apply it in graph problems.

pages.title: BFS Node Traversal Order
pages.content:
### BFS Node Traversal Order

BFS explores a graph level by level using a queue, while DFS explores as deeply as possible using recursion or a stack. With adjacency lists, both run in O(V+E).

callout.text: Use BFS Node Traversal Order to build a precise mental model of Graph Traversals, then apply it in graph problems.

pages.title: What is Connected Component
pages.content:
In a graph, a connected component is a set of vertices (nodes) where each vertex is connected to every other vertex in the set, directly or indirectly, through edges (connections). In simpler terms, it's a group of vertices that are all somehow reachable from one another within the graph. Connected components are useful for understanding the structure and connectivity of a graph, helping to identify groups of related nodes.

For example, in the given graph we have 3 connected components:

![CC](https://cdn.codechef.com/images/learning/graphs-trees/connected-components.png)

topics.title: Cycles in Graphs
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Cycles in Graphs.

pages.title: Cycles in Graphs
pages.content:
In graphs, a cycle is a series of edges that form a closed loop, where you can start and end at the same vertex by following the edges. In other words, you can travel through the graph, moving from one vertex to another along the edges, and eventually return to the starting vertex.

**Key points about cycles in graphs:**

1. **Closed Loop:** A cycle forms a closed loop, meaning there is no repetition of vertices (except for the starting and ending vertex) as you traverse the edges.

2 **Importance:** Cycles are significant in graph theory, and the presence or absence of cycles in a graph can determine its properties. Graphs without cycles are called acyclic, while those with at least one cycle are cyclic.

3. **Directed vs. Undirected Graphs:** Cycles can exist in both directed and undirected graphs. In a directed graph, the edges have a direction, and the cycle must follow the specified direction. In an undirected graph, the edges do not have a direction, and you can traverse them in either direction to form a cycle.

**Example:**
Consider the following undirected graph. We've a cycle with nodes `6`, `7` and `8` (6-7-8-6)

![ccbigraph](https://i.ibb.co/xgK9vTp/cycle-undirected-graph.png)

Similarly, in the following directed graph, we have a cycle with nodes `B`, `C`, `E` and `D` (B-C-E-D-B)

![ccunigraph](https://i.ibb.co/SXfpYfL/cycle-directed-graph.png)
